question: In order to complete a large job, 1000 workers were hired, just enough to complete the job on schedule. All the workers stayed on the job while the first quarter of the work was done, so the first quarter of the work was completed on schedule. Then 100 workers were laid off, so the second quarter of the work was completed behind schedule. Then an additional 100 workers were laid off, so the third quarter of the work was completed still further behind schedule. Given that all workers work at the same rate, what is the minimum number of additional workers, beyond the 800 workers still on the job at the end of the third quarter, that must be hired after three-quarters of the work has been completed so that the entire project can be completed on schedule or before?

First, there are 1000 workers hired initially, which is just enough to complete the job on schedule. So, the total work required is set such that 1000 workers can finish it exactly by the deadline. Then, during different quarters of the work, some workers are laid off, causing delays. We need to find out how many additional workers need to be hired after three-quarters of the work is done to get back on schedule.

Let me structure the problem. The job is divided into four quarters. Each quarter is 25% of the work. The first quarter was done with all 1000 workers, so that was completed on schedule. Then, after the first quarter, 100 workers are laid off, leaving 900. Then, after the second quarter, another 100 are laid off, leaving 800. The third quarter is done with 800 workers, and then after that, we need to hire additional workers beyond 800 to finish the last quarter on time.

So, after three quarters, we can hire more workers to speed up the last quarter. We need to find how many extra workers are needed so that the total time for all four quarters doesn't exceed the original scheduled time.

So, perhaps the key is to compute the time taken for each quarter with the varying number of workers, sum them up, and see how much time is left for the last quarter. Then, compute how many workers are needed to finish the last quarter in the remaining time.

But to do that, we need to relate the number of workers to the time taken. Since all workers have the same rate, we can use the concept of man-days or man-hours, but here it's about the rate of work.

The original schedule is with 1000 workers. Let’s compute the scheduled time for each quarter. Since the first quarter was completed on schedule with 1000 workers, the time taken for the first quarter is equal to the scheduled time for one quarter. Let’s call the total scheduled time T. Then each quarter is scheduled to take T/4 time.
